content: Team nursing is a historical approach to nursing care that operates on the principle of economy of scale. In this model, a single nurse or nursing assistant is assigned a specialized task for all patients within a hospital unit. For instance, one nurse might be responsible for administering and documenting all medications, while another focuses on checking and recording vital signs for the same group of patients. This method was initially developed under the direction of Eleanor Lambertson at Teachers College, Columbia University, with support from the Kellogg Foundation. However, the functional nursing model faced criticism for its fragmented care delivery, leading to the development of team nursing. The hallmark of team nursing is care through others, aiming to enhance patient satisfaction and address the shortcomings of functional nursing. It was designed to provide a more cohesive system of care, even amidst a shortage of professional nursing staff, by reducing the fragmented care associated with the functional model. Team nursing emerged in response to the social and technological changes during World War II, which drew many nurses away from hospitals. The increasing complexity and cost of medical procedures, equipment, and services necessitated specialization. This model sought to meet the growing demand for nursing services while optimizing the skills and knowledge of professional nurses. Definitions Team nursing is based on a philosophy where groups of professional and non-professional personnel collaborate to identify, plan, implement, and evaluate comprehensive, client-centered care. The core concept is teamwork, with all members working toward a shared goal of delivering high-quality, comprehensive nursing care. This model accommodates various personnel categories to meet the diverse nursing needs of a group of patients. Objectives of Team Nursing The primary objective of team nursing is to deliver the highest possible quality of patient care by fully utilizing the abilities of all staff members. This is achieved through close supervision of both patient care and the individuals providing it. Organizational Structure A clear organizational structure is essential for team nursing to ensure effective horizontal and vertical communication. This structure provides an organized framework for care delivery. Functioning of Team Nursing Two critical aspects of team nursing are: 1. The head nurse must always be aware of the patients' conditions and care plans, ensuring that assignments and work quality contribute to high standards of nursing care. 2. The team leader must have the autonomy to use their initiative, nurse patients, supervise, and teach without being burdened by administrative responsibilities. Role of Registered Nurses In team nursing, the registered nurse (RN) serves as the team leader, coordinating a small group of ancillary personnel (typically no more than four or five) to care for a small group of patients. The RN must be familiar with the condition and needs of all patients assigned to the team and plan individualized care for each. The team leader is also responsible for fostering a cooperative environment and maintaining clear communication among team members. Their duties include planning care, assigning tasks, directing and assisting team members, providing direct patient care, teaching, and coordinating patient activities. Team members report directly to the team leader, who then reports to the charge nurse or unit manager. Communication is facilitated through written patient assignments, nursing care plans, and regular team conferences to discuss patient status and revise care plans as needed. For team nursing to be effective, the team leader must possess strong clinical skills, excellent communication abilities, delegation skills, decision-making capabilities, and the ability to create a collaborative working environment. Communication Channels in Team Nursing Reports Work or assignment conferences Patient care conferences Written nursing care plans Team Conferences The team conference is a defining feature of team nursing. It typically consists of three parts: 1. Reports from each team member on their patients. 2. Planning for new patients and revising plans for existing ones as needed. 3. Planning the next day's assessments. The conference should be well-organized, concise yet comprehensive, and engaging. The team leader chairs the conference, providing an opportunity for all personnel to evaluate patient care and address problems through team discussions. Advantages of Team Nursing High-quality, comprehensive care can be delivered with a relatively high proportion of ancillary staff. Team members can participate in decision-making and problem-solving. Each team member can contribute their unique expertise or skills in patient care. Improved patient satisfaction. Organizational decision-making occurs at lower levels. Cost-effective system due to the expected ratio of unlicensed to licensed personnel. Effective in both inpatient and outpatient healthcare settings. Additional Advantages Promotes a sense of participation and belonging among team members. Workload can be balanced and shared. Division of labor allows members to develop leadership skills. Opportunities for team members to learn from and teach each other. Variety in daily assignments. Shared interest in the patient's well-being and care increases decision reliability. Nursing care hours are typically cost-effective. Patients can identify personnel responsible for their care. Continuity of care is enhanced, especially with consistent teams. Barriers between professional and non-professional workers are minimized, fostering group efforts. Everyone has the opportunity to contribute to the care plan. Disadvantages of Team Nursing Establishing a team concept requires time, effort, and consistent personnel. Simply assigning people to a group does not create a cohesive team. Unstable staffing patterns make team nursing challenging. All personnel must be client-centered. Reduced individual responsibility and independence in nursing functions. Continuity of care may suffer if daily team assignments vary, exposing patients to multiple caregivers. The team leader may lack the leadership skills necessary to effectively direct the team and foster a team spirit. Insufficient time for care planning and communication can lead to unclear goals, resulting in fragmented responsibilities and care. Modifications to Team Nursing To address its disadvantages, the team nursing model has undergone numerous modifications since its inception. Variations of the model are evident in other nursing care delivery methods, such as modular nursing. Modular Nursing Modular nursing is a variation of team nursing that focuses on the geographic location of patients for staff assignments. The patient unit is divided into modules or districts, with the same team of caregivers consistently assigned to the same geographic location. Each module has an RN as the team leader, with other team members potentially including LVNs/LPNs or UAPs. The team leader is accountable for all patient care and responsible for providing leadership and fostering a cooperative work environment. Modular nursing involves smaller groups of staff caring for smaller groups of patients, aiming to increase the RN's involvement in planning and coordinating care. Communication is more efficient among smaller groups of team members. Advantages of Modular Nursing Improved continuity of care when staff members are consistently assigned to the same module. The RN as team leader can be more involved in planning and coordinating care. Geographic proximity and efficient communication save staff time. Disadvantages of Modular Nursing Increased costs to stock each module with necessary patient care supplies (e.g., medication carts, linens, dressings). Long hospital corridors are not conducive to modular nursing.
